strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: improving generalization across tasks sharing a backbone. The proposed training procedure integrates with MGDA, PCGrad, CAGrad, and IMTL without changing the inference architecture.

Tables 1–4 show consistent aggregate improvements across classification and dense prediction benchmarks. For example, F-CAGrad raises MultiMNIST average accuracy from 95.01% to 95.95%, reduces CelebA error from 8.52% to 8.22%, and improves all three NYUv2 tasks relative to CAGrad.

The supplementary calibration results provide evidence beyond predictive accuracy: Brier scores and expected calibration errors improve across the three Multi-MNIST variants. Perturbation sensitivity and sharpness measurements further support investigating this approach.

Algorithm 1 makes the main procedure understandable. The supplement supplies architectures, optimizers, training schedules, and several repeated-run evaluations, while appropriately citing the underlying methods and datasets.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the central methodological contribution. Missing comparisons include directly aggregating per-task SAM gradients and applying SAM to a scalarized multi-task loss. There is also no ablation separating shared-parameter and task-head perturbations. Consequently, the results demonstrate benefits over conventional training but do not establish why the proposed separate aggregation of loss and flatness gradients is necessary.

The theoretical justification has substantive gaps. In Theorem 1 and Appendix A, componentwise maxima need not share a maximizing perturbation, so the vector bound does not establish the common worst-case perturbation asserted in the text. Algorithm 1 instead uses task-specific perturbations, and summing independently aggregated loss and flatness directions is not shown to preserve simultaneous descent. Appendix A also bounds Gaussian-tail contributions without stating the required bounded-loss assumption. The claimed theoretical support therefore needs more than editorial correction.

The evaluated implementation is insufficiently specified. Appendix B.2 states that experiments use adaptive SAM, whereas the main algorithm and derivation describe ordinary Euclidean SAM. The adaptation is not detailed, and the selected perturbation radii and validation selection procedure are not reported. Although the conclusion claims a public implementation, the supplied manuscript provides no repository link. Tables 2–4 also omit variability estimates needed to interpret smaller improvements.

Practical efficiency remains unestablished. Algorithm 1 requires additional gradient evaluations at task-specific perturbed parameters, which could be substantial for the 40-task CelebA setting. The paper reports neither runtime and memory overhead nor comparisons under matched computational budgets.

The interpretation sometimes exceeds the evidence. On NYUv2, F-MGDA improves the aggregate score while segmentation mIoU drops from 30.47 to 26.42, demonstrating a meaningful task trade-off rather than improvement for every task. The low-resource and noisy-label motivation is not directly tested; parameter perturbation experiments address a different robustness question. Moreover, the flatness visualizations do not clearly specify controls for parameter scaling, limiting their support for the proposed mechanism.
